lessons.title: RAM is your desk. Storage is your cabinet.
lessons.deck: Two kinds of space, two very different jobs.
lessons.summary: RAM holds what your Mac is actively working with; storage keeps things after the work is done. A crowded desk can slow you down even when the filing cabinet still has room, and an overfilled cabinet can leave the desk without a safe overflow area.

concepts.analogy: Your desk
concepts.definition: Fast, temporary memory used by apps and the system while they are running.
concepts.example: Open browser tabs, a design canvas, and the current video timeline all need room in RAM.

concepts.analogy: Your filing cabinet
concepts.definition: Long-term space on the SSD where apps, documents, photos, and system files remain.
concepts.example: A project stays on the SSD after you close its app or restart the Mac.

concepts.analogy: Everything spread across the desk right now
concepts.definition: The parts of open apps and files that the Mac needs to reach quickly at this moment.
concepts.example: Switching from browsing to editing video usually makes the working set much larger.

lessons.misconception: Adding more storage does not add more RAM. Free SSD space can help the Mac use swap safely, but RAM and storage remain separate resources.
lessons.takeaway: RAM is space for now; storage is space for later. Check which one is under pressure before deciding what to close or clean.

interaction.title: Set your workbench
interaction.prompt: Choose a workload and watch the active desk fill up.

lessons.title: When the desk gets crowded
lessons.deck: Memory pressure tells the fuller story; swap is the overflow plan.
lessons.summary: A low free-RAM number is not automatically bad. macOS intentionally uses available memory to work faster. Memory pressure combines several signals to show whether the system is coping comfortably or spending extra effort making room.

concepts.analogy: A traffic light for the desk
concepts.definition: A combined measure of how easily the Mac can meet current memory demand.
concepts.example: Green means the system is coping; sustained yellow or red suggests the active workload is too heavy.

concepts.analogy: An overflow box beside the desk
concepts.definition: SSD space temporarily used when active work cannot fit comfortably in RAM.
concepts.example: A background app may be moved to swap while a large edit stays ready in faster RAM.

concepts.analogy: Vacuum-packing papers before using another box
concepts.definition: A technique that packs inactive memory more tightly so more can remain in RAM.
concepts.example: The Mac may compress background app data before it begins swapping heavily.

lessons.misconception: Completely empty RAM is not the goal. The system uses spare RAM for useful work and cached data, then reclaims it when an app needs space.
lessons.takeaway: Watch sustained memory pressure and heavy swap—not free RAM by itself—when judging whether memory is the bottleneck.

lessons.title: How a file becomes a number
lessons.deck: Bytes measure content, while units and metadata explain why totals can differ.
lessons.summary: Every file is stored as bytes, but the number you see depends on how those bytes are counted and presented. Learning the units makes storage reports easier to compare without treating a harmless rounding difference as a mystery.

concepts.analogy: A tiny building block
concepts.definition: A basic unit of digital storage, made from eight bits.
concepts.example: A short text note needs thousands of bytes; a high-quality video may need billions.

concepts.analogy: Two measuring cups with slightly different marks
concepts.definition: A gigabyte uses powers of 1,000; a gibibyte uses powers of 1,024.
concepts.example: The same data can show a smaller number in GiB than in GB even though no bytes disappeared.

concepts.analogy: A luggage tag attached to the suitcase
concepts.definition: Information about a file, such as its name, dates, permissions, and location.
concepts.example: Two photos can contain similar pixels but have different dates, labels, and editing history.

lessons.misconception: A storage tool showing a different total is not necessarily wrong; it may use different units, rounding, permissions, or rules for shared data.
lessons.takeaway: Compare like with like: use the same units and the same scanning method when looking for real change.

lessons.title: The useful mess behind fast work
lessons.deck: Caches and build artifacts save time, but their copies can quietly accumulate.
lessons.summary: Many large folders are not personal documents. Apps and developer tools create local shortcuts and generated outputs so work opens or builds faster. These files may be rebuildable, but removing them still has a cost: the next launch or build may be slower and may need a network connection.

concepts.analogy: A shortcut drawer
concepts.definition: A stored copy of data that an app expects to use again soon.
concepts.example: A browser keeps image copies so a familiar page can load faster next time.

concepts.analogy: The cut pieces left beside a workshop project
concepts.definition: Generated output created while turning source files into a runnable app or other result.
concepts.example: Compiled objects, simulator builds, and preview outputs can be regenerated from source.

concepts.analogy: Each workshop keeping its own toolbox
concepts.definition: A local copy of third-party code or assets that a project needs to build.
concepts.example: Several projects may each keep their own package folder even when versions overlap.

lessons.misconception: Rebuildable does not mean worthless. Clearing a cache during active work can trade storage space for waiting, downloads, or a temporarily broken offline workflow.
lessons.takeaway: Treat generated data as reviewable, not disposable: confirm its owner, rebuild path, and timing before clearing it.

lessons.title: The app is only the front door
lessons.deck: An application, its settings, and your content often live in separate places.
lessons.summary: Dragging an app into the Trash removes its main application bundle, but that may be only part of its footprint. Preferences, downloads, libraries, plug-ins, and project data can live elsewhere so they survive updates or reinstalls.

concepts.analogy: The appliance itself
concepts.definition: The packaged program that appears as one app in Finder.
concepts.example: A creative app bundle contains its executable code, icons, and built-in resources.

concepts.analogy: The appliance's supply cupboard
concepts.definition: Data an app keeps outside its bundle to support features and future launches.
concepts.example: Downloaded models, templates, plug-ins, or content indexes may live there.

concepts.analogy: A labeled room with controlled doors
concepts.definition: A sandboxed area where an app stores its settings, caches, and local files.
concepts.example: Two apps can keep similarly named files separate because each has its own container.

lessons.misconception: Deleting an app does not guarantee that every related file is removed, and deleting every related folder can also remove work you meant to keep.
lessons.takeaway: Before removing an app, separate the program, its rebuildable support files, and your irreplaceable content.

lessons.title: Why free space can look slippery
lessons.deck: APFS can share capacity, reserve recoverable space, and preserve moments in time.
lessons.summary: Modern Macs use APFS, which manages storage more flexibly than a row of fixed boxes. Several volumes can share one container, some data can be reclaimed when needed, and snapshots can preserve earlier filesystem states. That flexibility is useful, but it makes one simple free-space number incomplete.

concepts.analogy: A building whose rooms share the same land
concepts.definition: A shared pool of disk capacity used by one or more APFS volumes.
concepts.example: System and Data volumes can report separately while drawing space from the same container.

concepts.analogy: A guest room that can be cleared when family arrives
concepts.definition: Locally stored data the system believes it can remove or download again when space is needed.
concepts.example: Some cached or cloud-backed files may count as used now but remain recoverable later.

concepts.analogy: A restore point in a time machine
concepts.definition: A read-only record of the filesystem state at a particular moment.
concepts.example: A local backup snapshot can help recover an earlier file version until the system releases it.

lessons.misconception: Two free-space readings that differ do not automatically mean disk corruption; they may count shared, purgeable, or snapshot data differently.
lessons.takeaway: Use free space as a trend, then inspect purgeable data and snapshots when the visible folders do not explain the total.

lessons.title: Find what changed, not only what is large
lessons.deck: A baseline and a repeatable scan turn storage cleanup into diagnosis.
lessons.summary: The largest folder today may have been large for years. To explain a sudden drop in free space, compare measurements taken the same way over time, then follow the categories with the biggest increase. This turns a vague feeling into a testable story.

concepts.analogy: The first mark on a measuring tape
concepts.definition: A trusted starting measurement used for later comparisons.
concepts.example: Record available space each morning before asking which category grew.

concepts.analogy: The distance between two marks
concepts.definition: The amount a measurement changed between snapshots.
concepts.example: If projects rose by 6 GB while free space fell by 7 GB, they are a strong lead—not yet proof.

concepts.analogy: How much of the map has street names
concepts.definition: The share of total change that a scan can explain with measured categories.
concepts.example: Low coverage means the report should say 'unknown' instead of guessing at protected or unscanned areas.

lessons.misconception: The biggest folder is not necessarily the cause of today's storage loss. Size answers 'what is large'; change answers 'what grew.'
lessons.takeaway: Measure consistently, compare deltas, and keep uncertainty visible. Diagnosis comes before cleanup.

lessons.title: Slow does not always mean busy
lessons.deck: Performance has several dimensions, and each points to a different fix.
lessons.summary: An app can feel slow because it is waiting, doing too much work, or handling work in large bursts. Separating responsiveness, latency, and throughput makes a vague complaint easier to investigate without assuming that one number explains everything.

concepts.analogy: How quickly a shopkeeper looks up when you speak
concepts.definition: How quickly a system reacts to an input and shows that it noticed you.
concepts.example: A button feels responsive when it acknowledges a tap immediately, even if the full result takes longer.

concepts.analogy: The travel time of a message
concepts.definition: The delay between requesting an operation and receiving its result.
concepts.example: A network request may have high latency when the server takes a noticeable moment to answer.

concepts.analogy: How many boxes a conveyor moves each minute
concepts.definition: The amount of work a system completes in a given period.
concepts.example: A build system has higher throughput when it can compile more files per minute.

lessons.misconception: A faster average does not guarantee a better experience. Rare long pauses can make an app feel worse even when most operations are quick.
lessons.takeaway: When something feels slow, ask whether the problem is reaction time, waiting time, or total work completed before choosing a fix.

lessons.title: A backup matters when it can come back
lessons.deck: A second copy is useful only when you know how to restore it.
lessons.summary: Backups reduce the risk of losing important work, but a backup is not the same as a pile of old files. You need a separate copy, a clear history of versions, and a small restore check so you know the protection works before an emergency.

concepts.analogy: A spare key kept somewhere safe
concepts.definition: A separate copy of data that can be used after loss, damage, or an unwanted change.
concepts.example: A project copy on an external drive can help after a laptop drive fails.

concepts.analogy: A stack of dated drafts
concepts.definition: Multiple preserved states of a file or project so you can recover an earlier version.
concepts.example: Version history can recover yesterday's spreadsheet after today's mistaken edit.

concepts.analogy: Trying the spare key before the lockout
concepts.definition: A small, deliberate check that confirms a backup can actually produce a usable file.
concepts.example: Restore one ordinary document to a temporary folder and open it to verify the path works.

lessons.misconception: A synced folder is not automatically a complete backup. A deletion or unwanted edit can synchronize too, and a backup you have never restored is an assumption rather than a tested recovery path.
lessons.takeaway: Keep an independent copy, preserve useful versions, and test a small restore occasionally. Protection includes the return trip.

lessons.title: A project is more than its folder
lessons.deck: Source files, generated outputs, and handoff notes each have a different job.
lessons.summary: Project hygiene is easier when you can tell what must be preserved, what can be rebuilt, and what another person or agent needs to continue. A tidy project is not merely small; it is understandable and recoverable.

concepts.analogy: The recipe card everyone trusts
concepts.definition: The canonical files and decisions used to explain or recreate a project.
concepts.example: Source code, a lockfile, and a short README can tell you what to change and how to rebuild it.

concepts.analogy: Sawdust left by the workshop
concepts.definition: Files produced from source material that can usually be recreated by a tool or build.
concepts.example: An Android build folder can be regenerated from the project source and its dependencies.

concepts.analogy: A note tied to the toolbox
concepts.definition: A compact record of context, decisions, checks, and the next action for whoever continues the work.
concepts.example: A handoff can name the changed files, the validation run, and the one open risk without copying the whole chat.

lessons.misconception: A small or clean-looking project is not automatically healthy. Missing setup instructions, ignored files, or undocumented decisions can make it harder to rebuild than a larger but explicit project.
lessons.takeaway: Preserve the source of truth, label rebuildable output, and leave a short handoff so the next session can start with context.

lessons.title: Private by keeping less
lessons.deck: Useful notes can answer the next question without keeping the whole conversation.
lessons.summary: Privacy is often improved before data is stored. Decide what the task actually needs, remove identifying detail from what remains, and give retained information a clear lifetime. Aggregate trends can be useful without preserving the source text.

concepts.analogy: Carrying only the keys you need today
concepts.definition: Collecting and retaining only the information required for a specific purpose.
concepts.example: A workflow report can keep category counts and time windows instead of raw prompts or message bodies.

concepts.analogy: Covering a name with an opaque marker
concepts.definition: Removing or masking details that are not needed for the intended use.
concepts.example: A diagnostic note can describe a permission error without including a personal path or secret token.

concepts.analogy: A library due date
concepts.definition: The defined period for keeping information before it is rotated, deleted, or summarized.
concepts.example: A dashboard may retain a short sequence of daily totals while discarding the raw observations.

lessons.misconception: Calling data aggregated does not make every dataset safe. Rare combinations of dates, places, or events can still identify someone, so aggregation should remove unnecessary detail as well as names.
lessons.takeaway: Start with the smallest useful record, strip identifying detail, and decide when the record should stop existing.

lessons.title: A good task leaves a trail
lessons.deck: Clear context turns one session into a reusable handoff.
lessons.summary: A task is easier to resume when the important context is captured before it disappears into a long session. A useful handoff names the goal, the current state, the checks that ran, and the next step without copying the whole conversation.

concepts.analogy: A labeled parcel
concepts.definition: A compact set of inputs, constraints, decisions, and current state needed to continue work.
concepts.example: A context packet can name the project goal, changed files, validation command, and one unresolved risk.

concepts.analogy: A trail marker
concepts.definition: A saved progress note made at a meaningful point so later work can restart from a known state.
concepts.example: After a working build, record what changed and what remains before beginning a larger refactor.

concepts.analogy: A receipt
concepts.definition: A short account of what was checked, how it was checked, and what result it produced.
concepts.example: A verification record can say that validation passed while a visual review still needs a screenshot.

lessons.misconception: A long transcript is not the same as usable context. Raw history can bury decisions, repeat stale assumptions, and retain details that the next task does not need.
lessons.takeaway: Before ending a task, leave the goal, changed files, checks, open risk, and next step. A small clear trail is more useful than a copied conversation.

lessons.title: The bottleneck can move
lessons.deck: A healthy diagnosis follows pressure between resources instead of trusting one number.
lessons.summary: An app can be limited by CPU, memory, storage, or the network, and the limiting resource can change as the workload changes. A short observation of what is waiting, what is busy, and what has headroom gives you a better next check than guessing from a single metric.

concepts.analogy: The narrowest part of a funnel
concepts.definition: The resource or step that currently limits how quickly the whole system can progress.
concepts.example: A build may have plenty of CPU available but still wait on a slow disk step.

concepts.analogy: Several people sharing one checkout
concepts.definition: Competition between tasks that need the same finite resource at the same time.
concepts.example: A browser, video export, and backup can contend for storage bandwidth even when each task is reasonable alone.

concepts.analogy: Empty seats kept for the next group
concepts.definition: Spare capacity that can absorb new demand before work starts queuing or failing.
concepts.example: Free storage gives updates and temporary files room to complete without an emergency cleanup.

lessons.misconception: Fixing the largest visible number does not always fix the symptom. Improving one resource can simply reveal the next bottleneck, so the workload and its waiting point still need checking.
lessons.takeaway: Ask what is waiting, what is saturated, and what has headroom. Follow the bottleneck as the workload changes.

lessons.title: Rebuildable is not disposable
lessons.deck: A safe cleanup decision includes ownership, timing, and a recovery path.
lessons.summary: Some files can be recreated, but that does not make every similarly named folder safe to remove. A careful cleanup identifies the exact allowlisted target, checks that the owner and rebuild path are understood, and stops when the permission boundary is unclear.

concepts.analogy: A guest list at the door
concepts.definition: An explicit set of paths or actions that a tool is permitted to handle.
concepts.example: A cleanup routine may allow a Gradle cache while excluding application data and source projects.

concepts.analogy: The recipe for making a replacement part
concepts.definition: The known steps and inputs needed to recreate generated data after it is removed.
concepts.example: A project-local build folder can be recreated by running the documented build with its lockfile and dependencies.

concepts.analogy: A locked gate around a work area
concepts.definition: The limit that determines whether a process may safely read, change, or remove a target.
concepts.example: An operation-not-permitted error is a signal to stop and report the boundary rather than try a broader command.

lessons.misconception: If a file looks generated, deleting it is automatically harmless. The name may hide important ownership, active work, or a missing recovery path.
lessons.takeaway: Delete only an exact approved target with a known rebuild path. When the boundary is unclear, preserve the data and report the blocker.

lessons.title: Make the next check testable
lessons.deck: A useful handoff turns uncertainty into one observable next action.
lessons.summary: Tasks become easier to resume when the next step is concrete enough to verify. Instead of leaving a vague instruction such as investigate further, name the condition to inspect, the small check to run, and the result that would change the plan.

concepts.analogy: The finish line painted on the track
concepts.definition: A clear condition that says what counts as complete or good enough.
concepts.example: A storage fix is complete when the approved routine finishes and the post-scan receipt is recorded.

concepts.analogy: A photograph of the trail marker
concepts.definition: An observable result that supports or challenges a conclusion.
concepts.example: A before-and-after measurement is evidence that a cleanup changed the intended category.

concepts.analogy: The next square in a board game
concepts.definition: The smallest specific step that moves the task forward and produces a useful result.
concepts.example: Run the validator and inspect the first reported error is more actionable than review the project.

lessons.misconception: More notes automatically make a handoff clearer. A long record can still hide the one decision, check, or blocker that matters next.
lessons.takeaway: Leave one observable next action, the evidence it should produce, and the condition that would change course.

lessons.title: A backup has more than one clock
lessons.deck: A copy is useful when its freshness and restore path fit the risk.
lessons.summary: A backup plan answers more than where a copy lives. It also answers how much recent work can be lost, how quickly the work must return, and whether the restore path has been tested. Those answers turn a reassuring copy into a usable recovery plan.

concepts.analogy: How many pages you can afford to lose from a notebook
concepts.definition: The maximum acceptable age of data that could be lost after a failure.
concepts.example: With a daily backup, a failure just before the next run could cost up to a day of recent project changes.

concepts.analogy: How long the shop can stay closed
concepts.definition: The maximum acceptable time to restore access to the work or service.
concepts.example: A personal archive may tolerate an afternoon of recovery, while a live service may need a much shorter plan.

concepts.analogy: Trying the spare key before the lockout
concepts.definition: A controlled check that a backup can be read and used to recover the intended data.
concepts.example: Restore one file or a small project copy to a temporary location and verify that it opens.

lessons.misconception: A successful backup job proves that recovery will work. A copy can be incomplete, inaccessible, too old, or missing the instructions needed to use it.
lessons.takeaway: Judge a backup by how fresh it is, how fast it can return the work, and whether a small restore has been tested.

lessons.title: A safe cleanup leaves a receipt
lessons.deck: A before-and-after record makes a small change easier to trust.
lessons.summary: Good cleanup is not only about removing files. It also records what was eligible, what changed, and what the follow-up scan found. That short receipt helps you distinguish a useful result from an accidental or unexplained change.

concepts.analogy: A guest list at the door
concepts.definition: An explicit set of targets that a tool is permitted to handle.
concepts.example: A routine can allow a rebuildable cache while leaving source projects, personal files, and app data outside its scope.

concepts.analogy: A photo taken before and after moving furniture
concepts.definition: Two comparable observations used to show what changed after an action.
concepts.example: A post-cleanup storage scan can show whether the approved target changed without claiming that every change came from the cleanup.

concepts.analogy: A store receipt for a careful purchase
concepts.definition: A compact record of the action, its scope, its result, and any remaining limitation.
concepts.example: A receipt can say that zero approved targets were present, so nothing was removed, while review-only categories stayed untouched.

lessons.misconception: A cleanup that reports zero removed bytes is not necessarily broken. An empty allowlist can be the correct result, and a permission boundary is a reason to stop rather than broaden the command.
lessons.takeaway: Define the target, measure the change, and record the result. A small receipt makes safe maintenance explainable and repeatable.

lessons.title: Memory is a working budget
lessons.deck: The useful question is whether active work has enough room to move.
lessons.summary: Memory is not a score to maximize or a shelf that should stay empty. The system uses it for active work, compression, and useful caches, then changes the mix as demand shifts. Looking at the workload and its pressure gives a better explanation than one free-memory number.

concepts.analogy: The tools spread across your desk for one job
concepts.definition: The data and code an active workload needs to access repeatedly right now.
concepts.example: Editing a large image can enlarge the working set even if the source file itself lives on storage.

concepts.analogy: A desk manager noticing that papers keep getting pushed aside
concepts.definition: A combined signal of how much effort the system is spending to satisfy current memory demand.
concepts.example: Sustained high pressure while several heavy apps are open is stronger evidence than a brief low-free-memory reading.

concepts.analogy: A clear corner reserved for the next tool
concepts.definition: Unused capacity that lets new work arrive without immediate queuing, swapping, or failure.
concepts.example: Leaving some memory and storage headroom gives a build room for temporary files and active compiler work.

lessons.misconception: More free memory is not automatically better, and adding storage does not increase RAM. Judge memory by sustained pressure and the workload's response, not by an isolated number.
lessons.takeaway: Treat memory as a working budget: identify the active workload, watch sustained pressure, and preserve enough headroom for the next step.

lessons.title: Generated files need a boundary
lessons.deck: A clean project keeps source, outputs, and local state easy to tell apart.
lessons.summary: Projects become easier to understand when the files you edit are separate from files tools create. A clear boundary protects source work, keeps reviews focused, and makes it safer to rebuild or remove generated outputs when they grow large.

concepts.analogy: The recipe card a kitchen agrees to follow
concepts.definition: The small set of human-maintained files that defines how a project should work.
concepts.example: A component file and its configuration may be the source of truth, while a compiled bundle is an output made from them.

concepts.analogy: The meal prepared from the recipe
concepts.definition: A file or folder produced by a tool from source inputs rather than edited as the primary project definition.
concepts.example: A build directory can be recreated from source and a lockfile, so it usually does not belong in the code review.

concepts.analogy: A sign showing which supplies stay off the shared counter
concepts.definition: A project rule that keeps local or generated files out of version control and routine review.
concepts.example: An ignore rule can exclude build output and local environment files while keeping the configuration template visible.

lessons.misconception: If a generated folder is large, deleting it is always the right first move. First confirm that it is reproducible, identify what creates it, and check whether any unusual local data is mixed in.
lessons.takeaway: Keep source, generated output, and local state distinct. That boundary makes collaboration, rebuilding, and safe maintenance easier.

lessons.title: Every project folder needs an owner
lessons.deck: A clear owner and lifecycle make project cleanup easier to trust.
lessons.summary: A large project folder is easier to maintain when you can answer four simple questions: who owns it, what creates each generated part, how it can be rebuilt, and when old output can be retired. Ownership turns an ambiguous pile of files into a system with decisions attached.

concepts.analogy: The person responsible for a shared workshop shelf
concepts.definition: A named person, team, or process responsible for deciding what a project folder contains and how it is maintained.
concepts.example: A project owner can confirm whether an old build is disposable or whether it is needed for a release comparison.

concepts.analogy: A tool's journey from new purchase to retirement
concepts.definition: The stages a file or folder passes through, such as creation, active use, archival, and removal.
concepts.example: A preview build may be active during a review, archived after approval, and removed once the source and release record are safe.

concepts.analogy: A recipe with exact ingredient versions written down
concepts.definition: A generated or maintained record that pins dependency versions so a project can be recreated more consistently.
concepts.example: A package lockfile helps a teammate reinstall the same dependency tree after a rebuildable folder is removed.

lessons.misconception: An ignore rule proves that a folder is safe to delete. It only says the folder is excluded from routine version control; ownership, rebuildability, and unusual local data still need checking.
lessons.takeaway: For every large project folder, identify its owner, generator, rebuild path, and retention decision before changing it.

lessons.title: Privacy starts before the report
lessons.deck: A privacy-safe workflow limits collection before it writes anything down.
lessons.summary: Privacy is easiest to protect when it shapes the measurement itself. Decide which fields are necessary, aggregate them at the source, keep a short retention window, and leave out content that does not improve the decision. A useful report can describe a pattern without preserving the material that produced it.

concepts.analogy: Packing only the tools needed for one repair
concepts.definition: Collecting and retaining only the smallest amount of information needed for a stated purpose.
concepts.example: A workflow report can keep category counts and shares without keeping prompts, message bodies, or file contents.

concepts.analogy: The label on a parcel rather than everything inside it
concepts.definition: Information about an item or activity, such as a timestamp, type, size, or title, rather than its full content.
concepts.example: A task type and local date can support an aggregate trend while the conversation itself remains unread and unrecorded.

concepts.analogy: A notice board that clears old notices regularly
concepts.definition: The defined period for keeping collected information before it is removed or replaced.
concepts.example: A fourteen-day summary window can show recent work patterns without becoming a permanent activity archive.

lessons.misconception: Data is private enough just because it stays on the same computer. Local files can still expose personal content, paths, names, or habits to anyone or any process that can read them.
lessons.takeaway: Choose the purpose first, aggregate early, retain briefly, and keep content out when metadata is enough.

lessons.title: A checkpoint is a promise to your future self
lessons.deck: Small, explicit checkpoints make unfinished work easier to resume safely.
lessons.summary: A useful checkpoint says what the work is trying to achieve, what has already been verified, and what remains uncertain. It does not need to preserve every detail. A short, current record gives the next session enough context to continue without guessing or repeating completed work.

concepts.analogy: A trail marker showing where to rejoin the path
concepts.definition: A small record of current state, completed verification, and the next safe action.
concepts.example: After a storage run, a checkpoint can record the snapshot compared, the cleanup result, and the alert that still needs attention.

concepts.analogy: A rule that must remain true while a room is rearranged
concepts.definition: A condition that should stay true before and after a change.
concepts.example: A cleanup invariant can be that review-only categories and files outside the allowlist remain untouched.

concepts.analogy: Passing a relay baton with the route and next stride clear
concepts.definition: A concise transfer of intent, evidence, constraints, and next action to another session or person.
concepts.example: A coding handoff can name the changed files, the passing test, the open edge case, and the command to run next.

lessons.misconception: A long transcript is automatically a good checkpoint. More history can make the important state harder to find and can preserve details that the next decision does not need.
lessons.takeaway: Record the goal, verified facts, constraints, open risk, and next action; keep the checkpoint short enough to trust.

lessons.title: A backup is only real when it comes back
lessons.deck: Restore practice turns a reassuring copy into usable protection.
lessons.summary: A backup can exist and still fail when you need it. The useful habit is to separate making a copy, keeping useful versions, and practicing a small restore. A simple restore drill can reveal missing permissions, incomplete files, expired retention, or a recovery process nobody remembers.

concepts.analogy: Trying the spare key before the front door is locked
concepts.definition: A planned check that retrieves selected data from a backup and confirms it is usable.
concepts.example: Restore one representative project file to a temporary folder and open it before relying on the backup for a larger recovery.

concepts.analogy: A shelf rule for how long old notebooks stay available
concepts.definition: The period during which backup versions are kept before they are replaced or removed.
concepts.example: A daily backup may protect recent edits while a monthly version preserves a longer-running history.

concepts.analogy: The last trail marker you can safely return to
concepts.definition: The time represented by the most recent usable backup version available for recovery.
concepts.example: If the last successful backup ran yesterday evening, changes made afterward may not be part of the available recovery point.

lessons.misconception: A backup job that reports success guarantees that recovery will work. Success may only mean that copying finished; it does not prove that the right data, permissions, and restore steps are usable.
lessons.takeaway: Keep backups with a clear retention plan and practice a small restore often enough that recovery is familiar.

lessons.title: Free space is headroom, not a finish line
lessons.deck: A little room lets ordinary work absorb temporary change safely.
lessons.summary: Free storage is useful because work is not perfectly still. Updates, exports, indexes, and temporary files all need room to appear before they are removed or moved elsewhere. The practical goal is enough headroom for the next normal task, not an empty disk.

concepts.analogy: The empty space above a box before the lid closes
concepts.definition: Capacity reserved for new or temporary work so the system does not operate at the edge.
concepts.example: An export may need temporary space even when the final video will be stored somewhere else.

concepts.analogy: A workbench copy used while making the final object
concepts.definition: A short-lived file created to support an operation such as editing, downloading, or building.
concepts.example: An installer can unpack files before it replaces an older application version.

concepts.analogy: A warning line on a measuring cup
concepts.definition: A chosen level at which a condition deserves attention or a different response.
concepts.example: A storage monitor can warn below a selected threshold while still leaving the decision to the person responsible.

lessons.misconception: The best storage state is an almost empty disk. A healthy system needs usable headroom, but the right amount depends on workload, update size, and recovery needs.
lessons.takeaway: Keep enough headroom for the next ordinary operation, and treat a threshold as a prompt to investigate rather than a reason to delete blindly.

lessons.title: Performance needs a bottleneck
lessons.deck: A useful diagnosis asks which limit is actually slowing the work.
lessons.summary: Performance is the result of a whole path: input, computation, memory, storage, and output. A fast component cannot remove a delay somewhere else in the path. Naming the current bottleneck makes the next measurement and fix much clearer.

concepts.analogy: The wait before a clerk starts serving you
concepts.definition: The time between requesting an operation and receiving its first useful response.
concepts.example: A command can have low total work but still feel slow if it waits a long time before showing anything.

concepts.analogy: How many parcels a loading dock handles per hour
concepts.definition: The amount of useful work completed in a unit of time.
concepts.example: A build system may improve throughput by compiling several independent files at once.

concepts.analogy: The narrowest part of a pipe
concepts.definition: The limiting part of a process that constrains the result of the whole system.
concepts.example: More CPU will not fix a process that spends most of its time waiting for a slow network response.

lessons.misconception: One impressive hardware number explains overall performance. The slowest relevant step can dominate the experience, and the bottleneck can move after a change.
lessons.takeaway: Measure the path, identify the current bottleneck, and verify that the next change improves the work that actually feels slow.

lessons.title: Backups need separation
lessons.deck: A second copy helps most when the same failure cannot remove both copies.
lessons.summary: A backup is a recovery option, not merely a duplicate with a different name. If the original and the copy share the same device, account, mistake, or failure mode, one event can affect both. Separation gives a backup a better chance to remain available when the original is not.

concepts.analogy: A spare bridge across the river
concepts.definition: Additional capacity or copies that can support recovery when one part fails.
concepts.example: Keeping another copy can preserve access if the primary drive stops working.

concepts.analogy: Two keys stored in different safe places
concepts.definition: The degree to which one copy can survive the failure, mistake, or access problem affecting another.
concepts.example: A backup on a separate device has more independence from a failure of the working drive.

concepts.analogy: Several dated drafts in a folder
concepts.definition: Multiple preserved points in time that allow recovery from deletion, corruption, or unwanted edits.
concepts.example: An older version can be useful when the newest synchronized copy contains an accidental change.

lessons.misconception: Two copies in the same place provide the same protection as two independent copies. Shared location, account, or automation can create one common failure point.
lessons.takeaway: Give important data a recovery copy with a meaningfully different failure path, and preserve enough versions for the mistakes you need to undo.

lessons.title: Project outputs need a home
lessons.deck: Clear boundaries make generated work easier to rebuild, review, and retire.
lessons.summary: A project is easier to maintain when source files, generated outputs, local settings, and release records have distinct homes. That separation reduces accidental commits, makes rebuilds more predictable, and gives old outputs a clear retention decision instead of leaving them in an unnamed pile.

concepts.analogy: A marked area where workshop scraps belong
concepts.definition: A deliberate separation between maintained inputs and files produced during a workflow.
concepts.example: A project can keep source in one directory and generated builds in a clearly named output directory.

concepts.analogy: A recipe another cook can follow
concepts.definition: The ability to recreate a result from recorded inputs, tools, and steps.
concepts.example: A lockfile and build instructions make it easier to recreate an output after the old build folder is removed.

concepts.analogy: A shelf label saying keep, archive, or recycle
concepts.definition: An explicit choice about how long a generated file should remain available and why.
concepts.example: A release archive may be retained for support while an experimental preview can expire after review.

lessons.misconception: Putting every generated file under version control is the safest way to preserve a project. Large outputs can hide the source of truth and make ordinary review harder.
lessons.takeaway: Give outputs a clear boundary, record how to recreate them, and attach a retention reason before they accumulate.

lessons.title: Privacy needs purpose limits
lessons.deck: A report is safer when every retained field has a job.
lessons.summary: Privacy is easier to maintain when collection starts with a narrow question. Keep only fields that answer that question, aggregate them before they become a history of individual activity, and define who or what can read the result. Less retained detail means fewer accidental disclosures to prevent.

concepts.analogy: A shopping list for one meal
concepts.definition: Collecting and using information only for a specific, stated need.
concepts.example: A storage trend needs byte counts and dates, not the names or contents of personal documents.

concepts.analogy: Counting boxes without opening them
concepts.definition: Combining individual observations into a summary that answers a question without preserving each detail.
concepts.example: A report can keep a category count for recent work instead of retaining each task's conversation.

concepts.analogy: A locked cabinet with a short guest list
concepts.definition: A technical or procedural limit on which people or processes can read a dataset.
concepts.example: A local dashboard can expose a summary while keeping raw activity records outside the dashboard data path.

lessons.misconception: A field is harmless because it seems small or ordinary. A collection of small fields can still reveal identity, habits, paths, or sensitive context when combined.
lessons.takeaway: State the purpose, aggregate early, keep retention short, and make the access boundary part of the design.

lessons.title: Agent work needs a next action
lessons.deck: A small, testable next step keeps delegated work easy to resume.
lessons.summary: Agent-assisted work becomes easier to trust when the handoff names the next action in plain language. The next action should fit the current constraints, produce observable evidence, and make it clear whether the task is complete or needs a different decision.

concepts.analogy: The destination written on a travel card
concepts.definition: The outcome the work is meant to achieve, separate from the steps used to reach it.
concepts.example: The intent may be a validated data refresh, while the exact files changed are implementation details.

concepts.analogy: The guardrails along a mountain road
concepts.definition: A condition that limits which actions are allowed or which result is acceptable.
concepts.example: A cleanup constraint can forbid touching personal files even if they are large.

concepts.analogy: Checking the address before handing over a parcel
concepts.definition: A concrete check that shows whether the intended result was achieved without breaking an invariant.
concepts.example: Running the validator and checking the changed-file list can verify both data shape and scope.

lessons.misconception: A detailed plan is always a better handoff than one clear next action. Too many speculative steps can hide the current decision and make resumption less safe.
lessons.takeaway: Write the intent, preserve the constraints, and leave one small verification step that tells the next session what to do.

lessons.title: Memory has layers
lessons.deck: Fast working space, helpful copies, and overflow space each play a different role.
lessons.summary: A computer's memory story is not one bucket called free or full. Active data may be held in fast working memory, repeated data may be kept in a cache, and less-active data may move to slower storage-backed space. The useful question is which layer is carrying the pressure and what the workload feels like.

concepts.analogy: The tools currently on the desk
concepts.definition: Fast memory used for data and instructions the system needs to access actively.
concepts.example: A running editor keeps the current document and nearby operations ready in working memory.

concepts.analogy: A shelf of frequently used supplies
concepts.definition: Stored data kept because it may be useful again, but which can usually be recreated or replaced.
concepts.example: A browser may cache images so a familiar page opens faster on a later visit.

concepts.analogy: Moving rarely used papers into a nearby archive box
concepts.definition: Moving less-active memory between fast working memory and slower storage-backed space.
concepts.example: The system may page background data out of fast memory so an active operation can continue.

lessons.misconception: A cache or a large amount of storage-backed memory is equivalent to adding physical RAM. These layers can help the system cope, but they have different speed and capacity tradeoffs.
lessons.takeaway: Separate working memory, useful caches, and paging when diagnosing a slowdown; the layer under pressure determines the sensible next check.

lessons.title: Snapshots need the same lens
lessons.deck: A storage trend is useful only when each reading measures comparable ground.
lessons.summary: A daily storage reading is one measurement at one moment, not a diagnosis by itself. Comparing snapshots is useful when they use the same roots, exclusions, units, and timing. If the scan changes, a category can appear to grow or shrink even when the files did not.

concepts.analogy: The first photograph in a before-and-after pair
concepts.definition: A reference measurement used to judge a later change.
concepts.example: Yesterday's post-cleanup snapshot can be the baseline for today's storage comparison.

concepts.analogy: The distance between two marks on a ruler
concepts.definition: The difference between two measurements made with the same method.
concepts.example: A positive free-space delta means today's reading has more available storage than the baseline.

concepts.analogy: The shaded portion of a map
concepts.definition: The portion of the measured space that a scanner could account for under its rules.
concepts.example: A scan that measures Projects but excludes restricted system locations has partial coverage of the disk.

lessons.misconception: A larger category in the latest report proves that its files grew. A changed scan scope, permission boundary, unit, or attribution rule can change the number without the underlying files changing.
lessons.takeaway: Compare like-for-like post-cleanup snapshots, keep coverage visible, and treat a changed measurement method as part of the explanation.

lessons.title: Storage needs a retention reason
lessons.deck: A clear reason to keep a file is more useful than a vague fear of deleting it.
lessons.summary: Storage decisions get easier when each file or folder has a job, an owner, and a reason to remain. Source material may need careful preservation, while generated outputs may need a shorter review window. Naming the reason makes cleanup safer because it separates important history from rebuildable residue.

concepts.analogy: A library rule for how long a book stays on the shelf
concepts.definition: The decision about how long information should remain available and under what conditions.
concepts.example: A release record may be retained for support while a temporary preview can be removed after review.

concepts.analogy: The master recipe behind many plated meals
concepts.definition: The maintained input that should be trusted when recreating or checking a result.
concepts.example: Source code and a lockfile can be the source of truth for a generated build folder.

concepts.analogy: A route back to the workshop
concepts.definition: The documented inputs and steps needed to recreate a generated result.
concepts.example: A project note can name the command, dependencies, and configuration needed to recreate a preview.

lessons.misconception: Keeping every output forever is the safest form of preservation. Unnamed copies can hide the maintained source, consume space, and make it harder to identify which result is trustworthy.
lessons.takeaway: For anything you keep, name its purpose; for anything you remove, confirm the source of truth and rebuild path first.

lessons.title: Performance needs a small experiment
lessons.deck: A narrow comparison teaches more than a long list of guesses.
lessons.summary: Performance work is easier to reason about when one suspected bottleneck is changed at a time and the result is checked with the same task. This turns a feeling such as ‘it is slow’ into a comparison that can support the next decision without pretending that one example measures every workload.

concepts.analogy: The narrowest part of a funnel
concepts.definition: The resource or step that most limits the speed of the current workload.
concepts.example: A slow disk read can limit an export even when the processor is not fully busy.

concepts.analogy: A starting line before a race
concepts.definition: A recorded reference result made before a change.
concepts.example: Time the same representative action once before changing a cache or rendering path.

concepts.analogy: Changing one ingredient while keeping the recipe the same
concepts.definition: A comparison where the important conditions stay consistent except for the factor being tested.
concepts.example: Use the same input and verification step when comparing two implementation choices.

lessons.misconception: A faster result in one run proves the whole system is faster. Background activity, warm caches, input differences, and measurement noise can change a single observation.
lessons.takeaway: Name the suspected bottleneck, keep the comparison narrow, and record enough context to repeat the check.

lessons.title: Backups need a restore check
lessons.deck: A backup becomes trustworthy when you can recover a useful piece from it.
lessons.summary: A backup can exist without being ready for recovery. A file may be incomplete, an account may have lost access, or the restore steps may be unclear. A small, safe restore check tests the path while the original data is still available and turns a hopeful copy into a more understood recovery option.

concepts.analogy: Taking a book back off the emergency shelf
concepts.definition: Recovering usable data from a backup or other preserved copy.
concepts.example: Open a recovered document in a separate location and confirm that it is usable.

concepts.analogy: A sealed parcel arriving with its contents intact
concepts.definition: The condition that preserved data remains complete and unchanged in the ways that matter for recovery.
concepts.example: A restore check can confirm that a project archive contains the expected files and opens correctly.

concepts.analogy: An evacuation map posted before the alarm
concepts.definition: The ordered steps, access details, and decisions needed to recover from a failure.
concepts.example: A short note can record where the copy lives, which account can access it, and how to restore one item.

lessons.misconception: A successful backup job proves that recovery will work. Copying can finish while access, completeness, encryption keys, or restore instructions still have a problem.
lessons.takeaway: Test a small restore periodically, keep the recovery steps with the backup plan, and treat the result as evidence rather than a promise.

lessons.title: Projects need a clean boundary
lessons.deck: Keep source, generated output, and personal scratch space easy to tell apart.
lessons.summary: A project is easier to understand when its durable source is separated from files a tool can regenerate and from private scratch material. Clear boundaries make storage reports more useful, make handoffs safer, and reduce the chance that a cleanup or rebuild removes something that carried meaning.

concepts.analogy: The signed master recipe
concepts.definition: The durable files that explain how a project is meant to work and can be used to recreate its result.
concepts.example: A repository's source code and configuration should explain how to rebuild the app even if generated folders are absent.

concepts.analogy: A printed copy made from the recipe
concepts.definition: A file or folder produced by a tool from source material rather than authored as the primary record.
concepts.example: A build folder can be recreated from the project's source and dependencies after a clean checkout.

concepts.analogy: A labeled shelf between shared supplies and private notes
concepts.definition: A clear rule about what belongs to the project, what can be rebuilt, and what should remain personal or temporary.
concepts.example: A short README and ignore rule can keep local experiments out of the shared source while leaving the rebuild path visible.

lessons.misconception: A folder being inside a project does not make every file equally important. Some files define the work, some are generated from it, and some are private context that should not be copied or deleted casually.
lessons.takeaway: Name the source of truth, mark generated output, and keep personal scratch space outside the shared boundary whenever possible.

lessons.title: Privacy needs a data boundary
lessons.deck: A useful report can stay useful without carrying the private material behind it.
lessons.summary: Privacy improves when a workflow collects only what its decision needs, turns individual records into safe totals before sharing them, and removes detail when its purpose is finished. The goal is not to make every report empty; it is to keep the report useful while leaving private source material at home.

concepts.analogy: Packing only what you need for a short trip
concepts.definition: Collecting and retaining no more personal information than the stated purpose requires.
concepts.example: A workflow dashboard can record category counts without copying prompts, message bodies, or file contents.

concepts.analogy: Watching the shape of a crowd from a distance
concepts.definition: Combining individual records so a report describes a pattern instead of exposing each activity.
concepts.example: A report can say that seven recent tasks carried a research signal without listing the task titles.

concepts.analogy: A pantry shelf with an expiry label
concepts.definition: A rule for how long collected information remains available before it is replaced or removed.
concepts.example: A rolling fourteen-day summary can be refreshed from current metadata instead of keeping an ever-growing activity log.

lessons.misconception: Removing a person's name makes any remaining data private. Rare combinations of timing, paths, titles, or other details can still identify an activity or reveal more than the report needs.
lessons.takeaway: Set the purpose first, collect the minimum, aggregate before sharing, and give the remaining detail a clear retention limit.

lessons.title: Agent work needs a stop condition
lessons.deck: A task is easier to trust when it says what finished looks like.
lessons.summary: Agent work can wander when the desired result, verification step, or boundary is left implicit. A small stop condition makes the work easier to review: state the outcome, check the important invariant, and stop when the agreed scope is met. This keeps a useful task from turning into unrequested changes or endless polishing.

concepts.analogy: The final item on a packing list
concepts.definition: A concrete condition that shows the requested result is present and usable.
concepts.example: A dashboard task can require that the approved data files validate and that unrelated files remain unchanged.

concepts.analogy: A guardrail that stays in place while the road changes
concepts.definition: A property that must remain true before, during, and after a change.
concepts.example: A privacy invariant can require that a report contain aggregate counts but no prompt bodies, secrets, or file contents.

concepts.analogy: A marked turn-around point on a trail
concepts.definition: A stated point at which the task is complete or must pause for a new decision.
concepts.example: Once the requested files pass validation and the named comparison is reported, further cleanup requires a separate request.

lessons.misconception: More work after the requested result is always safer or more helpful. Extra investigation or polishing can expand scope, alter unrelated state, and make the original result harder to review.
lessons.takeaway: Define the result, name the invariant to protect, and treat the stop condition as part of the task rather than an afterthought.

lessons.title: Memory needs a working set
lessons.deck: The useful question is what must stay ready for the current job.
lessons.summary: A computer does not need every file open at once. It needs the active pieces of the current job close at hand, while less urgent pieces can wait. Thinking in terms of a working set makes memory conversations more practical than chasing an empty-memory number.

concepts.analogy: The pages spread across a desk
concepts.definition: The data and code an active workload needs to reach quickly.
concepts.example: A browser with several active tabs and a design editor may need a larger working set than a text note.

concepts.analogy: A helper working in the next room
concepts.definition: A running task that supports the system or an app without being the current foreground action.
concepts.example: Indexing or syncing can use memory while you edit a document.

concepts.analogy: How crowded the desk feels while you work
concepts.definition: A combined signal of how easily the system is meeting current memory demand.
concepts.example: Sustained pressure during the same task is more useful evidence than one momentary free-memory reading.

lessons.misconception: The largest possible amount of free RAM is not the goal. Memory used for useful caches and active work can be reclaimed when another task needs it.
lessons.takeaway: Describe the current workload, watch sustained pressure, and treat free RAM as context rather than a target score.

lessons.title: Storage cleanup needs a receipt
lessons.deck: A clear record makes a reversible cleanup easier to trust.
lessons.summary: Cleaning storage changes the evidence you will use later. A receipt preserves what was selected, why it was allowed, and how much space the operation reported. That record helps separate an intentional rebuild from an accidental disappearance.

concepts.analogy: A store receipt for a return
concepts.definition: A small record of what a cleanup operation changed and what it reported reclaiming.
concepts.example: A receipt can group reclaimed bytes by approved target without listing private file contents.

concepts.analogy: A guest list at a door
concepts.definition: An explicit set of targets that an operation is permitted to touch.
concepts.example: A safe routine may allow rebuildable build output while leaving personal folders outside the list.

concepts.analogy: The instructions for making a replacement part
concepts.definition: The known steps and source needed to recreate removed generated data.
concepts.example: A project can document the command or tool that regenerates a build folder after cleanup.

lessons.misconception: A larger reclaimed number does not make a cleanup safer. Scope, ownership, and a usable rebuild path matter as much as the bytes reported.
lessons.takeaway: Keep a concise receipt, name the allowlist, and make the rebuild path understandable before trusting a cleanup.

lessons.title: Performance starts with a baseline
lessons.deck: A before-picture gives a later result something honest to compare with.
lessons.summary: When an app feels slow, memory, storage, network, and application work can all be suspects. A baseline records one representative action before a change. Repeating that action afterward makes the result easier to discuss without pretending one example measures every device or workload.

concepts.analogy: A starting mark on a ruler
concepts.definition: A reference observation made before changing the system or workload.
concepts.example: Record how long the same export takes before trying a new setting.

concepts.analogy: A sample slice of the whole cake
concepts.definition: A small action chosen because it resembles the work that actually matters.
concepts.example: Use the project’s normal preview action instead of an unrelated toy example.

concepts.analogy: A second hand moving the finish line
concepts.definition: Another change that can affect the observation besides the factor being tested.
concepts.example: A background update or a warm cache can change one run even when the code is unchanged.

lessons.misconception: One faster run proves a lasting improvement. Background work, input differences, and cache state can influence a single observation.
lessons.takeaway: Choose a representative task, record a baseline, repeat the same check, and describe the result as evidence from that example.

lessons.title: A backup needs a job
lessons.deck: A copy is easier to trust when you know what failure it is meant to cover.
lessons.summary: Different copies protect against different problems. A recent working copy can help with accidental edits, while a separate historical copy can help with a larger failure. Naming the job of each backup makes gaps visible without requiring a complicated system.

concepts.analogy: The emergency each tool is packed for
concepts.definition: The specific loss or recovery need a preserved copy is intended to address.
concepts.example: A daily copy may focus on recovering yesterday’s project after an accidental change.

concepts.analogy: A saved chapter in a book
concepts.definition: The moment in time represented by a recoverable copy.
concepts.example: A copy from last night represents a different recovery point from one made last month.

concepts.analogy: The kind of storm a shelter is built for
concepts.definition: The event or mistake that could make the original data unavailable or wrong.
concepts.example: Device loss and accidental deletion are different failure modes with different recovery needs.

lessons.misconception: Having one copy somewhere does not prove that every important failure is covered. The copy may be too old, too close to the original, or unable to restore the needed item.
lessons.takeaway: Name the failure a backup covers, the recovery point it represents, and the smallest restore that would prove it useful.

lessons.title: Project hygiene needs an ignore rule
lessons.deck: A clear rule keeps generated noise from becoming part of the durable project.
lessons.summary: Projects often create local output that is useful on one machine but not part of the source. An ignore rule expresses that boundary to version-control tools and to future collaborators. It is a small piece of documentation about what should be rebuilt instead of shared.

concepts.analogy: A sign saying ‘leave this in the workshop’
concepts.definition: A rule that tells a version-control tool not to treat matching local files as ordinary project changes.
concepts.example: Generated build output can stay local when the project already has a documented rebuild path.

concepts.analogy: An item written into the shared ledger
concepts.definition: A file recorded by version control as part of the project’s change history.
concepts.example: Source code and configuration are usually tracked so another checkout can reproduce the work.

concepts.analogy: Packing slips mixed into the recipe box
concepts.definition: Recreated or machine-specific output that obscures the meaningful project changes.
concepts.example: A local build folder can make a review harder to read when it appears beside a small source edit.

lessons.misconception: Ignoring a path does not make its contents safe to delete. A generated folder can still contain useful local evidence or an unusual artifact that should be preserved separately.
lessons.takeaway: Use ignore rules to state the project boundary, then keep the rebuild path and any exceptional local data visible.

lessons.title: Privacy is more than redaction
lessons.deck: Removing a name is not the same as collecting only what the task needs.
lessons.summary: A report can still reveal private activity through timing, rare combinations, or unnecessary detail even after obvious names are removed. Privacy starts earlier: define the purpose, collect the smallest useful fields, and aggregate them before they leave the working context.

concepts.analogy: Black ink over a sentence
concepts.definition: Removing or hiding selected details from information that was already collected.
concepts.example: A report may remove a personal name from a line while leaving the unusual timestamp visible.

concepts.analogy: Packing only the tools needed for one repair
concepts.definition: Collecting and keeping no more information than the stated purpose requires.
concepts.example: A workflow summary can keep category totals without copying message bodies.

concepts.analogy: Footprints that connect separate paths
concepts.definition: The ability to connect records that were intended to be viewed separately.
concepts.example: A rare project name and a precise time can link an aggregate entry back to one activity.

lessons.misconception: Anonymizing one field makes the whole report anonymous. Several harmless-looking fields can combine into a revealing description.
lessons.takeaway: Minimize at collection time, aggregate before sharing, and remove details that do not change the decision.

lessons.title: Agent work needs right-sized evidence
lessons.deck: Verification should be large enough to support the claim and small enough to stay understandable.
lessons.summary: A useful agent result connects each important claim to a fitting check. A focused test can support a narrow change, while a broader request needs broader verification. Choosing the smallest evidence that answers the real question keeps work reviewable and avoids collecting unrelated private detail.

concepts.analogy: A sentence in a witness statement
concepts.definition: A specific statement about what changed, what is true, or what was observed.
concepts.example: ‘The approved data files validate’ is a narrower claim than ‘the whole application is healthy.’

concepts.analogy: Checking the lock after saying the door is closed
concepts.definition: A deliberate check that tests whether a claim holds under the relevant conditions.
concepts.example: A schema validator is fitting evidence for a data-shape claim.

concepts.analogy: Using a key cut for the right lock
concepts.definition: The degree to which a check covers the same boundary as the claim it supports.
concepts.example: A file-level test may not support a claim about unrelated deployment behavior.

lessons.misconception: More logs or more checks automatically make a result more trustworthy. Unrelated evidence can expose private detail while still failing to test the important claim.
lessons.takeaway: State the claim, choose a check with the same scope, and keep evidence no broader than the decision requires.

lessons.title: Memory has warm and cold data
lessons.deck: Not every piece of an open workload needs the same kind of attention.
lessons.summary: Some data is used repeatedly and benefits from staying close to the processor; other data can wait until it is needed. The warm-and-cold distinction helps explain why systems keep caches and why an inactive app can still have a smaller memory cost than its full contents would suggest.

concepts.analogy: Tools already laid out for the next step
concepts.definition: Data that a current workload is likely to use soon or repeatedly.
concepts.example: The visible portion of a working document may be warmer than an unopened section.

concepts.analogy: Supplies stored on a high shelf
concepts.definition: Data that is not currently needed and can wait before being brought close to active work.
concepts.example: An inactive tab may have much of its state kept out of the immediate working set.

concepts.analogy: Keeping errands in the same neighborhood
concepts.definition: The tendency for a workload to reuse nearby or recently used data.
concepts.example: Editing one part of a file repeatedly benefits from keeping related data close together.

lessons.misconception: An app’s total file size tells you exactly how much memory it needs right now. Active use, access patterns, and shared data change the working set.
lessons.takeaway: Ask which data is active, which can wait, and how the workload moves between them before judging memory use.

lessons.title: Storage counts files as well as bytes
lessons.deck: A folder with many small items can behave differently from one large file.
lessons.summary: Storage reports emphasize bytes, but file count and directory structure also affect indexing, backup traversal, and everyday navigation. This does not make file count a replacement for size; it adds another clue when a folder feels cumbersome despite not being the largest one.

concepts.analogy: The number of boxes in a room
concepts.definition: How many separate filesystem items a folder or tree contains.
concepts.example: A source tree with many tiny generated files can be slower to inspect than one archive of similar total size.

concepts.analogy: Checking each label before moving a shipment
concepts.definition: Work involving names, dates, permissions, and locations rather than file contents alone.
concepts.example: A backup tool may need to visit many file entries even when each file is small.

concepts.analogy: A filing cabinet with nested drawers
concepts.definition: The hierarchy of folders and files used to organize a filesystem.
concepts.example: Deep generated nesting can make ownership and cleanup scope harder to see.

lessons.misconception: A folder with fewer bytes is always easier for every tool to handle. Many entries and deep nesting can create work that a byte total does not show.
lessons.takeaway: Use bytes to understand capacity, and use file count and structure when diagnosing indexing, backup, or navigation friction.

lessons.title: Performance can benefit from batching
lessons.deck: Doing related small actions together can change the cost of the whole trip.
lessons.summary: Repeated small operations can spend time on setup, handoff, or waiting between each item. Batching combines related work so that overhead is paid less often. The tradeoff is that a large batch can delay feedback or use more memory, so the right size depends on the task.

concepts.analogy: Taking one full shopping trip instead of many single-item trips
concepts.definition: Grouping related operations so shared setup or transfer work happens fewer times.
concepts.example: Processing several small files in one command can reduce repeated startup overhead.

concepts.analogy: The time spent opening the shop before each sale
concepts.definition: Work required to start, coordinate, or finish an operation beyond its main useful result.
concepts.example: A request may have a fixed connection cost before it transfers its actual data.

concepts.analogy: Waiting for the whole tray before tasting one cookie
concepts.definition: The time between starting grouped work and seeing a useful partial or final result.
concepts.example: A very large batch may use fewer startups but make an error harder to notice early.

lessons.misconception: A bigger batch is always faster. Batching can increase memory use, delay feedback, and make a failure harder to isolate.
lessons.takeaway: Compare grouped and individual work on the real task, then choose a batch size that balances overhead with timely feedback.

lessons.title: Backups need readable restore points
lessons.deck: A preserved copy is easier to use when its time and contents are clear.
lessons.summary: When several copies exist, a vague label can turn recovery into guesswork. A restore point should tell you roughly when it was made, what it contains, and how it differs from nearby copies. Clear names reduce the chance of restoring the wrong state or overwriting a useful one.

concepts.analogy: A bookmark with a chapter title
concepts.definition: A preserved state that can be selected as the source for recovery.
concepts.example: A project copy labeled with its date and purpose is easier to distinguish from a test archive.

concepts.analogy: An expiry note on a pantry jar
concepts.definition: Information that explains how long a copy should remain available or why it is kept.
concepts.example: A release archive may be kept for a different reason from a short-lived daily copy.

concepts.analogy: A spare table for unpacking a parcel
concepts.definition: The separate location where recovered data is placed for inspection or use.
concepts.example: Restoring into a new folder lets you compare the recovered document before replacing the current one.

lessons.misconception: The newest copy is automatically the right copy. It may contain a mistake, be incomplete, or serve a different recovery purpose.
lessons.takeaway: Label restore points by time and purpose, inspect them in a separate destination, and keep the original until recovery is understood.

lessons.title: Project dependencies need owners
lessons.deck: A dependency is easier to maintain when someone can explain why it exists and how it is refreshed.
lessons.summary: Third-party packages, SDKs, and generated assets can become invisible project weight when nobody owns the decision around them. Recording the purpose, version rule, and update path makes upgrades safer and makes stale or duplicate copies easier to review.

concepts.analogy: A borrowed tool needed to finish the job
concepts.definition: External code, data, or tooling that a project relies on to build or run.
concepts.example: An application may depend on a library for parsing, rendering, or network access.

concepts.analogy: A shopping list with exact brands and sizes
concepts.definition: A file that records resolved dependency versions so installs can be reproduced more consistently.
concepts.example: A clean checkout can use the lockfile to recreate the intended package set.

concepts.analogy: A label naming who maintains a shared tool
concepts.definition: A short explanation of why a dependency exists and who decides when it changes.
concepts.example: A project note can explain which feature needs a package and what check should follow an upgrade.

lessons.misconception: A dependency is harmless because it can be installed again. Version drift, unavailable sources, and incompatible updates can still make a rebuild different.
lessons.takeaway: Record why a dependency exists, pin the intended version where appropriate, and name the check that follows an update.

lessons.title: Privacy includes metadata
lessons.deck: The label around a file can reveal as much as the file’s visible content.
lessons.summary: Names, paths, timestamps, permissions, and counts can describe a person’s work even when the content is never opened. A privacy-aware workflow treats metadata as data, too, and keeps only the fields needed for the decision.

concepts.analogy: The address label on a sealed parcel
concepts.definition: Information that describes an item, such as its name, size, time, owner, or location.
concepts.example: A folder name and modification time can reveal a project activity without exposing its files.

concepts.analogy: Guessing the event from footprints outside
concepts.definition: A conclusion someone can draw from details that were not intended to answer that question directly.
concepts.example: A sequence of timestamps may suggest a person’s schedule even when each record looks ordinary.

concepts.analogy: Choosing only the columns needed on a form
concepts.definition: The deliberate choice of which data fields a workflow will read, retain, or share.
concepts.example: A dashboard may need a category count but not the original path or exact time.

lessons.misconception: A workflow is private because it never reads file contents. Metadata can still expose identity, timing, location, or habits.
lessons.takeaway: Review names, paths, times, and counts as carefully as content, and omit fields that do not change the decision.

lessons.title: Agent work separates observation and action
lessons.deck: Knowing what is present and deciding what to change are different steps.
lessons.summary: A safe workflow first gathers enough evidence to describe the current state, then applies a narrowly authorized change, and finally checks the result. Keeping those phases distinct makes it easier to see what the system was like before the action and what the action actually changed.

concepts.analogy: Taking a photograph before moving furniture
concepts.definition: A read-only description of the current state or evidence.
concepts.example: A storage scan can record category sizes before any cleanup is attempted.

concepts.analogy: A fence around the approved garden bed
concepts.definition: The explicit limit on which actions and targets a task may affect.
concepts.example: A safe routine can allow rebuildable caches while excluding personal files and source code.

concepts.analogy: Checking the room after the furniture move
concepts.definition: A property that should be true after the authorized action completes.
concepts.example: A post-cleanup scan can confirm the receipt and show that review-only categories remain present.

lessons.misconception: A plausible guess about the state is enough to justify the action. Without an observation and a boundary, a helpful-looking change can affect the wrong target.
lessons.takeaway: Observe first, name the authorization boundary, act once, and verify the postcondition.
