lessons.title: Background work still has a cost
lessons.deck: Quiet helpers can compete with the task you can see.
lessons.summary: Syncing, indexing, backups, and updates often run without a visible window. They can use memory, processor time, storage activity, or network capacity while a foreground task is waiting. Recognizing background work helps explain why the same action can feel different at different times.

concepts.analogy: A kitchen preparing ingredients while the dining room is open
concepts.definition: System or app work that continues while another task is in the foreground.
concepts.example: A search index can update while you continue editing a note.

concepts.analogy: Two people reaching for the same narrow doorway
concepts.definition: Competition between workloads for a shared resource.
concepts.example: A backup and a video export may contend for storage bandwidth.

concepts.analogy: A time when the workshop is between deliveries
concepts.definition: A period chosen to reduce unrelated activity while a task is observed.
concepts.example: A repeatable comparison may be easier when scheduled outside a known indexing window.

lessons.misconception: If no window is visible, no other work is using the device. Background activity can be real without being foregrounded.
lessons.takeaway: When timing matters, note background activity and compare the same task during a reasonably quiet period.

lessons.title: Recovered storage can be temporary
lessons.deck: Free space is a state that can change again as tools rebuild their working data.
lessons.summary: Removing rebuildable data can create breathing room, but the next build, launch, or sync may recreate part of it. A cleanup is easier to evaluate when the receipt is compared with later snapshots, so regrowth becomes information instead of a surprise.

concepts.analogy: A lawn growing back after mowing
concepts.definition: The return or increase of generated data after it was removed.
concepts.example: A build cache can grow again after a project is compiled on a fresh machine.

concepts.analogy: A dated photograph of the room
concepts.definition: A measurement captured at a particular time for later comparison.
concepts.example: A daily storage snapshot can show whether a cleared category stays small or returns quickly.

concepts.analogy: The water level after the faucet and drain balance
concepts.definition: A recurring range a system tends to return to under similar work.
concepts.example: A project may settle into a familiar cache size after several normal builds.

lessons.misconception: The space reclaimed immediately after cleanup is a permanent reduction. Rebuildable data may return because the work that needs it returned.
lessons.takeaway: Record the cleanup, watch later snapshots, and judge storage pressure by the trend rather than one moment.

lessons.title: Performance is a responsiveness contract
lessons.deck: People need feedback while work is happening, not only a fast final number.
lessons.summary: A task can finish quickly and still feel poor if the interface stops acknowledging input. Responsiveness is about the conversation between a person and a system: notice the action, show progress when useful, and complete the work without making the user guess whether anything happened.

concepts.analogy: A person nodding to show they heard you
concepts.definition: How quickly and clearly a system acknowledges an input.
concepts.example: A button can respond immediately with a state change even if the final operation continues.

concepts.analogy: A delivery tracker on a long trip
concepts.definition: Information that shows ongoing work is active and what remains understandable.
concepts.example: A progress state can distinguish a slow operation from an unresponsive one.

concepts.analogy: The time until the parcel arrives
concepts.definition: The delay between starting an operation and receiving its completed result.
concepts.example: An export can acknowledge the request quickly while its completion still takes time.

lessons.misconception: Responsiveness and total completion time are the same thing. Fast acknowledgement can improve trust even when the underlying work cannot finish immediately.
lessons.takeaway: Measure both acknowledgement and completion, then give the person clear feedback during unavoidable waits.

lessons.title: Backups test the inconvenient path
lessons.deck: The recovery step that is easiest to ignore is often the one worth rehearsing.
lessons.summary: A happy-path backup check can miss the conditions that make recovery difficult: a different machine, a missing account, an old version, or a single important file. A small rehearsal of the awkward step exposes unclear instructions while the original data is still available.

concepts.analogy: A fire drill before the alarm
concepts.definition: A controlled practice of recovering a limited item or state from a preserved copy.
concepts.example: Restore one ordinary project file to a separate destination and open it.

concepts.analogy: The key needed to open the emergency cabinet
concepts.definition: An account, credential, device, or permission required before recovery can begin.
concepts.example: A backup may be intact but unusable if nobody knows which account can reach it.

concepts.analogy: A missing plank in a bridge
concepts.definition: A weakness that prevents a preserved copy from becoming usable recovered data.
concepts.example: An undocumented encryption key or unavailable application can create a recovery gap.

lessons.misconception: A backup is validated because its job completed without an error. The real test includes access, selection, restoration, and opening the recovered result.
lessons.takeaway: Rehearse one inconvenient recovery step, record what was unclear, and improve the procedure while the source remains safe.

lessons.title: Clean checkouts clarify projects
lessons.deck: A fresh rebuild can separate source problems from local residue.
lessons.summary: Local projects accumulate caches, generated output, and machine-specific settings. A clean checkout or clean build removes some of that history and asks whether the documented source is sufficient. It is a diagnostic tool, not a reason to delete a working environment without a recovery plan.

concepts.analogy: Cooking from a new copy of the recipe
concepts.definition: A project working tree created from the recorded source without relying on old local output.
concepts.example: A clean checkout can reveal that a build depends on an undocumented local file.

concepts.analogy: Getting the same meal from the same recipe
concepts.definition: The ability to recreate a result from the stated inputs and steps.
concepts.example: A documented dependency set makes a fresh build more reproducible than a machine-specific setup.

concepts.analogy: Old ingredients left on the counter
concepts.definition: Generated or machine-specific state left by earlier work that is not part of the durable source.
concepts.example: A stale generated file can hide a missing source configuration until a clean build is attempted.

lessons.misconception: A clean checkout is always safe to perform immediately. It can expose missing documentation and may require network access, credentials, or time to rebuild.
lessons.takeaway: Use clean builds as diagnostics, keep the working copy recoverable, and document every input the fresh result needs.

lessons.title: Privacy gives summaries a scope
lessons.deck: A summary is safer when its audience, purpose, and detail are explicit.
lessons.summary: Aggregation reduces detail, but it does not remove the need for boundaries. A useful summary says what period and population it describes, who needs it, and what it intentionally leaves out. Those limits help readers avoid treating a narrow pattern as a complete personal record.

concepts.analogy: The frame around a group photo
concepts.definition: The defined time range, population, and grouping rules behind an aggregate result.
concepts.example: A fourteen-day category count does not describe every task or every month.

concepts.analogy: A room with a named guest list
concepts.definition: The limit on who should receive or interpret a report.
concepts.example: A private dashboard may be appropriate for an owner but not for a public status page.

concepts.analogy: A map showing the roads it does not cover
concepts.definition: A plain statement of important details the summary intentionally does not include.
concepts.example: A workflow report can state that it excludes prompts, message bodies, secrets, and file contents.

lessons.misconception: An aggregate number speaks for everything that happened. It only describes the records and scope used to produce it.
lessons.takeaway: Name the scope, audience, and omissions so a useful summary does not become an overconfident personal profile.

lessons.title: Agent handoffs need a next check
lessons.deck: A handoff is stronger when the next person knows how to resume and verify it.
lessons.summary: A handoff should carry the current state, the boundary that was protected, and the next check that matters. This keeps another person or agent from repeating exploration, guessing at unfinished work, or expanding scope simply because the stopping point was unclear.

concepts.analogy: A trail marker left for the next hiker
concepts.definition: A concise record of what was done, what remains, and what context is needed to continue.
concepts.example: A note can identify the validated files, the comparison still needed, and the protected boundaries.

concepts.analogy: A bookmark placed at the next paragraph
concepts.definition: The specific place and state from which follow-up work should begin.
concepts.example: A task can resume at the post-change verification instead of repeating the initial scan.

concepts.analogy: A labeled envelope waiting for an answer
concepts.definition: A remaining uncertainty that needs evidence or a decision before the work can expand.
concepts.example: A handoff can say that a review-only category needs a separate decision without touching it now.

lessons.misconception: A long activity log is a good handoff. Volume can hide the current state, the protected boundary, and the one check that matters next.
lessons.takeaway: Leave the current state, protected boundary, resume point, and next verification in a compact handoff note.

lessons.title: Memory needs a working-set story
lessons.deck: A memory reading makes sense when you connect it to the work the system is keeping ready.
lessons.summary: Memory is not a simple empty-versus-full gauge. The useful question is which active pieces of work must stay quickly available, how much the system can compress, and whether it is repeatedly moving data to slower storage. A small working-set story turns a scary number into a testable explanation.

concepts.analogy: The papers currently spread across a desk
concepts.definition: The data and code an active workload needs to access frequently during a period of work.
concepts.example: A browser with many live tabs and a video editor open at once has a larger working set than either app alone.

concepts.analogy: Folding clothes before filling the suitcase
concepts.definition: A technique that stores some in-memory data in a smaller form so more active work can fit in RAM.
concepts.example: The system may compress inactive app data before it needs to use the SSD as overflow.

concepts.analogy: Moving a rarely used folder to a nearby cabinet
concepts.definition: Moving a memory page from RAM to storage so RAM can serve other active work.
concepts.example: If a background app is paged out, returning to it may take longer while its data comes back.

lessons.misconception: A high memory-use percentage alone proves that the Mac is in trouble. The stronger signal is sustained pressure, heavy paging, or noticeable responsiveness problems during the workload.
lessons.takeaway: Describe the active working set and watch pressure over time before deciding whether memory needs attention.

lessons.title: Free space needs a buffer
lessons.deck: Headroom gives ordinary work somewhere to go when a task briefly gets larger.
lessons.summary: Free storage is not only a number to admire after cleanup. It is working room for updates, exports, temporary files, and the system's own housekeeping. Keeping a buffer makes normal changes less stressful, while a threshold gives you a prompt to inspect the trend without pretending it identifies the cause.

concepts.analogy: Empty seats kept for late arrivals
concepts.definition: Capacity intentionally left available so ordinary work can handle temporary increases.
concepts.example: A video export may need temporary working files even when the final video is smaller than the available space.

concepts.analogy: A fuel warning light
concepts.definition: A chosen boundary that prompts attention when a resource gets close to a less comfortable range.
concepts.example: A dashboard can flag a low free-space threshold so you compare recent snapshots before deciding what deserves review.

concepts.analogy: Walking distance from the edge of a crowded platform
concepts.definition: The amount of room between the current state and a meaningful limit.
concepts.example: The same 5 GB change leaves a very different margin when free space starts at 100 GB versus 12 GB.

lessons.misconception: Crossing a free-space threshold proves which folder caused the change or makes deletion safe. It is a signal to compare like-for-like readings and review approved evidence.
lessons.takeaway: Keep a useful buffer, treat thresholds as prompts, and investigate the measured change before choosing a safe next action.

lessons.title: Performance needs a baseline
lessons.deck: A baseline turns a vague feeling of slowness into a comparison you can repeat.
lessons.summary: Performance work becomes clearer when you first describe a normal run, then change one meaningful factor, and finally compare the same signal again. A baseline does not promise a perfect explanation, but it keeps impressions from becoming unsupported claims and helps a small experiment teach you something useful.

concepts.analogy: A starting line painted on a track
concepts.definition: A recorded reference condition used to compare later behavior.
concepts.example: Before changing a build setting, record how long the same clean build takes under the usual project conditions.

concepts.analogy: Turning one tap while keeping the others still
concepts.definition: An experiment that changes one relevant factor while keeping the comparison conditions as similar as practical.
concepts.example: Compare two cache configurations with the same input, device state, and number of runs.

concepts.analogy: A clock that shows the same time when checked the same way
concepts.definition: A measurement that can be collected again using a defined procedure and unit.
concepts.example: Use elapsed seconds for the same operation instead of relying only on whether it felt faster today.

lessons.misconception: One faster run proves that a change improved performance. A single result can be noise, warm-up, or a different workload, so the comparison needs a defined baseline and repeatable conditions.
lessons.takeaway: Record a baseline, change one relevant factor, and repeat the same measurement before drawing a performance conclusion.

lessons.title: Backups need a recovery window
lessons.deck: A backup plan is easier to trust when you know how far back it can actually take you.
lessons.summary: A backup is useful when it covers the kind of mistake you are preparing for and can be restored within the time you need. Think about the last usable version, how long versions remain available, and whether a small restore check has confirmed the path. The exact schedule is a choice for the work, not a promise supplied by the word backup.

concepts.analogy: A bookmark in the history of a notebook
concepts.definition: The point in time represented by a copy that you could restore.
concepts.example: A nightly backup can represent the previous evening's state, which may be enough for some work but not for every kind of change.

concepts.analogy: A shelf that holds only a chosen number of boxes
concepts.definition: The period during which backup versions remain available for recovery.
concepts.example: Keeping seven daily versions can help with a recent mistake while offering less protection for a problem discovered much later.

concepts.analogy: Trying the spare key before the door is urgent
concepts.definition: A deliberate check that a backup can be found, opened, and used to recover something small.
concepts.example: Restoring a test file or following a documented drill can reveal a missing permission or an unclear step before a real recovery.

lessons.misconception: Having a recent backup automatically means every important change is protected and the copy will be easy to restore. Coverage, retention, and a tested recovery path still matter.
lessons.takeaway: Choose the recovery window for the work, keep versions long enough for the likely mistake, and test a small restore path.

lessons.title: Project hygiene needs a boundary
lessons.deck: A clear line between source, output, and scratch work makes a project easier to resume.
lessons.summary: A project is easier to understand when its essential source files are distinct from generated results and temporary experiments. That boundary helps you decide what must be preserved, what can be rebuilt, and what another person or agent needs to continue without guessing.

concepts.analogy: The recipe and ingredients
concepts.definition: A canonical input, decision, or configuration used to recreate the intended result.
concepts.example: Application code, a lockfile, and a documented configuration can explain how to rebuild a project.

concepts.analogy: The baked loaf made from the recipe
concepts.definition: A result produced from source files that can usually be recreated by running the right process.
concepts.example: A build folder or compiled bundle may be useful for testing but should not replace the source of truth.

concepts.analogy: The workbench beside the kitchen
concepts.definition: Temporary files and experiments that support a task without being part of the durable project record.
concepts.example: A one-off export or a local test fixture can stay outside the handoff until it is either documented or discarded.

lessons.misconception: A smaller project folder is automatically a healthier project. Removing generated results or undocumented experiments can erase useful context or make the next rebuild harder.
lessons.takeaway: Mark what is source, generated, and scratch; preserve the source of truth and leave a short handoff note for anything another person must reproduce.

lessons.title: Privacy needs a retention window
lessons.deck: Keeping less data means deciding how long a useful record should remain.
lessons.summary: A record can be private today and still create future risk if it is kept longer or in more detail than its job requires. A retention window names how long a useful record should remain, while aggregation can preserve a trend without preserving the underlying activity. The goal is a deliberate, limited record rather than automatic erasure or permanent collection.

concepts.analogy: A library loan period
concepts.definition: The chosen period for keeping a record before it is reviewed, reduced, or removed.
concepts.example: A model dashboard might keep daily storage totals for a 90-day review window, then remove older totals when they no longer serve that purpose.

concepts.analogy: Packing only the tools needed for one repair
concepts.definition: Collecting and keeping only the data needed for a stated task.
concepts.example: A workflow summary can count task records without keeping the prompts, message bodies, or file contents.

concepts.analogy: A weather report instead of every raindrop
concepts.definition: Combining detailed observations into a less identifying summary.
concepts.example: A report can show how many tasks occurred in a period without listing the titles or words from those tasks.

lessons.misconception: Private means that data is harmless to keep forever, while deletion is always the safest answer. A record can be useful for a limited purpose, and keeping more detail or more history than needed can increase exposure.
lessons.takeaway: Name the purpose, keep the smallest useful summary, and set a review point for how long it should remain.

lessons.title: Agent work needs a small proof
lessons.deck: A compact verification step makes delegated work easier to trust and resume.
lessons.summary: When an agent changes something, the most useful handoff is not a long account of every action. It is a clear result, the boundary that was respected, and one small check that supports the result. This keeps follow-up focused and makes it easier to spot when a task needs another look.

concepts.analogy: A receipt attached to a delivered package
concepts.definition: A small piece of evidence that a stated result or constraint was checked.
concepts.example: A validation command passing can support a claim that a data-file change still matches the project schema.

concepts.analogy: A fence around the part of a garden being tended
concepts.definition: The explicit limit on which files, systems, or decisions a task is allowed to affect.
concepts.example: A cleanup task can name its approved rebuildable targets while leaving source code and personal files outside the work.

concepts.analogy: A bookmark with a note about the next paragraph
concepts.definition: A short handoff statement that identifies the current state and the next useful check.
concepts.example: A note can say that the safe scan finished, the dashboard files were refreshed, and the next run should compare the next daily snapshot.

lessons.misconception: More activity detail makes agent work more trustworthy. A long log can still hide what changed, what was protected, and how to verify the result.
lessons.takeaway: State the result, name the protected boundary, and leave one small proof point and next check for whoever resumes the work.

lessons.title: Memory needs a foreground budget
lessons.deck: The task in front of you shares the machine with work happening behind the scenes.
lessons.summary: Memory use is shaped not only by the app you opened but also by the background work sharing the machine. A useful check names the foreground task, notices the largest competing work, and compares the same condition after one change. This gives you a clearer next step than closing things at random.

concepts.analogy: The main customer at a counter
concepts.definition: The app or task you are actively trying to keep responsive right now.
concepts.example: When editing a photo, the editor and the image you are working on form the foreground workload.

concepts.analogy: Orders waiting behind the counter
concepts.definition: Ongoing work that is not the current interaction but still uses system resources.
concepts.example: A sync job, indexer, or project build can continue using memory while you work in another app.

concepts.analogy: A tray with room reserved for the main order
concepts.definition: A practical plan for leaving enough working memory for the task that matters most.
concepts.example: Before starting a large export, pause an unneeded build and close only the largest unrelated workload.

lessons.misconception: The number of open apps alone explains whether memory is under pressure. A small set of apps can hold large working sets, while background work and the current task also affect what the system must keep ready.
lessons.takeaway: Name the foreground task, identify the biggest competing workload, and compare the same condition after one deliberate change.

lessons.title: Storage alerts need a crossing
lessons.deck: A threshold is useful when you know whether the reading just crossed it or has been there for a while.
lessons.summary: A low-space number deserves context. Compare today's reading with the previous daily snapshot and ask whether it newly crossed a threshold, stayed below it, or recovered above it. That distinction prevents a persistent condition from being reported as a new event and keeps attention on real changes.

concepts.analogy: A line painted across a trail
concepts.definition: A chosen boundary at which a reading deserves a different kind of review or response.
concepts.example: A storage policy can use 20 GB free or 15% available as a line for closer review.

concepts.analogy: Stepping through a doorway
concepts.definition: A change from one side of a threshold to the other between two comparable readings.
concepts.example: If free space was above 20 GB yesterday and below it today, the threshold was newly crossed.

concepts.analogy: The previous mark on a ruler
concepts.definition: A reference reading used to understand the current value and its change.
concepts.example: The previous distinct daily snapshot can serve as today's baseline for the free-space difference.

lessons.misconception: Any reading below an alert threshold is a new alert. If the device was already below it, the useful new information may be the direction and size of change, not a newly crossed condition.
lessons.takeaway: Compare today with the previous distinct reading, separate threshold crossings from persistent states, and describe the change before choosing a next check.

lessons.title: Performance needs a smallest bottleneck
lessons.deck: The slowest part of a workflow often sets the pace for everything around it.
lessons.summary: When a task feels slow, start by finding the step that is limiting progress right now. A faster processor, a larger cache, or a more elaborate setup may not help if the real wait is a network response, one busy disk, or a single serial step. Name the repeated wait, change one thing, and measure the same step again.

concepts.analogy: The narrow neck of a bottle
concepts.definition: The part of a process that limits how quickly the whole process can move.
concepts.example: A build with many quick tasks can still feel slow when one signing step waits on a single device or service.

concepts.analogy: The pause before a reply
concepts.definition: The time between asking for an operation and receiving its first useful response.
concepts.example: A file browser can feel unresponsive when each folder change waits on a remote location, even if later transfers are fast.

concepts.analogy: How many boxes pass a loading dock per hour
concepts.definition: The amount of work completed over a period of time.
concepts.example: A photo export may have good throughput once it starts while still having noticeable latency before the first preview appears.

lessons.misconception: The most visible resource is always the bottleneck. High CPU, memory use, or disk activity can be a consequence of useful work while the real limit sits in a different step.
lessons.takeaway: Describe the repeated wait, identify the step that limits progress, change one variable, and compare the same measure again.

lessons.title: Backups need a separate destination
lessons.deck: A second copy helps only when it is separate enough from the original problem.
lessons.summary: A backup is more useful when it has a different failure path from the data it protects. A second folder on the same disk may help with an accidental edit, but it cannot help if that disk fails. Think about what could go wrong, place the copy where that problem does not reach both versions, and check that the copy can be opened.

concepts.analogy: A spare key kept outside the locked room
concepts.definition: A separate copy of data kept so it can be recovered after loss, damage, or an unwanted change.
concepts.example: A project copy on an external drive can help if the working drive is damaged.

concepts.analogy: The route a leak takes through a building
concepts.definition: The chain of shared conditions that can cause multiple copies or systems to fail together.
concepts.example: Two folders on one drive share the drive's failure path, while a copy on another device may avoid it.

concepts.analogy: Trying the spare key before an emergency
concepts.definition: A small test that confirms a backup exists in a usable form and can produce the needed data.
concepts.example: Opening a backed-up document or restoring a small test folder can reveal whether the copy is readable.

lessons.misconception: Having two copies automatically means the data is safely backed up. If both copies share the same disk, account, location, or untested format, one problem can still affect both.
lessons.takeaway: Name the failure you are guarding against, keep a copy outside that failure path, and perform a small restore check.

lessons.title: Project hygiene needs a rebuild note
lessons.deck: A short recipe makes generated work easier to remove, replace, and trust.
lessons.summary: Generated files are easier to manage when a project explains how to recreate them. A small rebuild note can name the required tools, the expected command, and the output location. That context turns an opaque folder into a replaceable result and helps the next person—or your future self—tell safe cleanup from lost work.

concepts.analogy: A recipe taped inside the workshop door
concepts.definition: A brief record of the inputs and steps needed to recreate a generated result.
concepts.example: A project note can say which command recreates a preview bundle and where that bundle appears.

concepts.analogy: The ingredients measured before cooking
concepts.definition: A tool, dependency, setting, or input that must be available before a rebuild can succeed.
concepts.example: A particular runtime version or environment variable may be required before a local build works.

concepts.analogy: A photocopy that can be made again from the original page
concepts.definition: Generated data that can be safely recreated from preserved source files and known steps.
concepts.example: A compiled preview can be removed when its source and rebuild instructions are still available.

lessons.misconception: A folder is not safely disposable just because it looks generated. Without preserved inputs and a working rebuild path, deleting it may turn a replaceable result into lost work.
lessons.takeaway: Before clearing generated project data, confirm the source, prerequisites, command, and output location are documented well enough to rebuild it.

lessons.title: Privacy starts with a purpose
lessons.deck: A clear reason helps you choose what a useful record should leave out.
lessons.summary: Privacy is easier to protect when a record has a specific job. Start by naming the decision the record should support, then keep only the smallest details needed for that decision. A useful aggregate can show a trend without preserving the activity that produced every point.

concepts.analogy: Packing for one short trip
concepts.definition: Collecting and using information only for a stated, appropriate purpose.
concepts.example: A storage dashboard can keep category totals for trend review without keeping filenames or document text.

concepts.analogy: Using the smallest useful measuring cup
concepts.definition: Choosing the least amount of information that can still support the task.
concepts.example: A workflow report can count task records and dates while omitting prompts, message bodies, and secrets.

concepts.analogy: A class attendance total instead of every student's route
concepts.definition: A combined summary that preserves a useful pattern while reducing detail about individual events.
concepts.example: A weekly task count can reveal activity volume without listing the individual tasks.

lessons.misconception: Keeping data local automatically makes every detail safe to retain. Local data still deserves a purpose, a limited scope, and a plan for how long it should remain.
lessons.takeaway: Name the decision a record supports, keep the smallest useful summary, and leave out details that do not serve that purpose.

lessons.title: Agent work needs a checkpoint
lessons.deck: A small handoff marker keeps a long task understandable when work pauses.
lessons.summary: Agent work can span many steps, but a useful checkpoint does not need to list every thought or action. It records the current result, the boundary that still matters, and the next verification step. That compact marker makes a paused task easier to resume and review.

concepts.analogy: A trail marker at the last safe crossing
concepts.definition: A brief record of the current state that supports a later continuation or review.
concepts.example: A checkpoint can say that the approved files were refreshed, validation is next, and source files were not touched.

concepts.analogy: Trying the door before declaring the room finished
concepts.definition: A small test tied directly to the intended result or constraint.
concepts.example: Running the project validator checks that a dashboard update still follows its schema.

concepts.analogy: Passing a baton with the next runner's lane visible
concepts.definition: A concise transfer of status, evidence, and next action to another person or process.
concepts.example: A handoff can identify the changed report, the passing check, and the one comparison the next run should make.

lessons.misconception: A longer activity log is automatically a better handoff. Detail without a clear result, boundary, and next check can make the important information harder to find.
lessons.takeaway: Leave a checkpoint with the result, the protected boundary, one proof point, and the smallest useful next action.

lessons.title: Memory benefits from a smaller working set
lessons.deck: Reducing what must stay ready can help the current task remain responsive.
lessons.summary: When memory pressure persists, the useful question is which work must remain ready right now. Keep the foreground task's data close, then pause or close the largest unrelated work only when that change is safe. Comparing the same workload afterward gives a better signal than chasing an empty-memory number.

concepts.analogy: Tools spread across today's workbench
concepts.definition: The data and code an active task needs readily available during a period of work.
concepts.example: A large image editor, its source files, and an export preview can form the working set for a design task.

concepts.analogy: Two people reaching for the same tool
concepts.definition: Competition between tasks for the same limited system resource.
concepts.example: A project build and a video export may contend for memory while both keep large intermediate data ready.

concepts.analogy: Putting away one tool before opening another
concepts.definition: Reducing resource demand through one deliberate, reversible change.
concepts.example: Pausing an unneeded build before a large export is a controlled reduction that can be tested and reversed.

lessons.misconception: Closing many small apps is always the best memory fix. The largest working set or background job may matter more, and random changes make it harder to learn what helped.
lessons.takeaway: Protect the foreground task, identify the biggest competing working set, change one thing, and compare the same condition again.

lessons.title: Storage growth needs a trail
lessons.deck: A sequence of comparable readings explains change better than one impressive total.
lessons.summary: Storage diagnosis becomes clearer when each reading has the same lens: the same categories, units, and approximate timing. The difference between two readings shows what moved, while the category breakdown suggests where to look next. A single large total cannot tell you whether growth is new or longstanding.

concepts.analogy: The distance between two marks on a ruler
concepts.definition: The numerical change between a current measurement and its reference measurement.
concepts.example: A category that grows from 8 GB to 10 GB has a positive delta of 2 GB.

concepts.analogy: Sorting a receipt into the right shopping bags
concepts.definition: Assigning measured change to the category or source that best explains it.
concepts.example: A repeatable scan can attribute growth to project data, app data, or rebuildable caches without inspecting file contents.

concepts.analogy: Using the same starting line for every race
concepts.definition: A prior measurement collected with sufficiently similar rules to support a fair comparison.
concepts.example: The previous distinct daily snapshot is a better baseline than an older reading made with different scan coverage.

lessons.misconception: The largest category today is automatically the cause of a recent storage problem. Size and growth are different questions, and only a comparable baseline reveals the change.
lessons.takeaway: Keep the scan lens consistent, compare deltas, and follow the categories with meaningful new growth rather than the categories that are merely large.

lessons.title: Performance needs a repeatable test
lessons.deck: A small controlled comparison separates a real improvement from a lucky run.
lessons.summary: A workflow can feel faster for many reasons, including a warm cache, a quieter machine, or a smaller input. A repeatable test keeps the task, input, and measurement close enough that one change can be judged fairly. The goal is not perfect laboratory precision; it is a trustworthy comparison.

concepts.analogy: A marked stretch of road for testing a car
concepts.definition: A repeatable workload and measurement used to compare performance.
concepts.example: Running the same build command on the same project before and after one change creates a simple benchmark.

concepts.analogy: Keeping the other knobs still
concepts.definition: A condition held steady so the effect of one chosen change is easier to see.
concepts.example: Using the same input files and build mode controls the comparison when testing a tool change.

concepts.analogy: Small waves around an average waterline
concepts.definition: Natural variation between repeated measurements of the same process.
concepts.example: A few seconds of difference across identical runs may be ordinary variance rather than a meaningful regression.

lessons.misconception: One faster run proves that a change improved performance. A single result can be noise, so repeat the same test and look for a consistent direction.
lessons.takeaway: Choose one workload, hold the important conditions steady, repeat the measurement, and change one variable at a time.

lessons.title: Backups need a recovery map
lessons.deck: A backup is useful when you know what it can restore and how long that path takes.
lessons.summary: A backup plan becomes practical when it names the data to recover, the copy to use, and the steps that connect the two. Different failures call for different recovery paths: a deleted file, a damaged drive, and a lost account do not all use the same copy. A small test can reveal missing instructions before an emergency.

concepts.analogy: The last saved page in a notebook
concepts.definition: The latest moment in time represented by a usable backup copy.
concepts.example: A nightly backup may restore yesterday's project but not edits made this morning.

concepts.analogy: How long it takes to find the spare key and open the door
concepts.definition: The time needed to make the required data usable again after a failure.
concepts.example: Restoring one document may take minutes, while rebuilding a full workstation can take much longer.

concepts.analogy: A checklist for rebuilding a campsite
concepts.definition: The ordered steps used to retrieve data, restore prerequisites, and verify the result.
concepts.example: A restore sequence may recover the project, reinstall its dependencies, and then open a known test file.

lessons.misconception: A backup is proven by the fact that a copy exists. Without knowing its recovery point, steps, and usability, the copy may not meet the need when something fails.
lessons.takeaway: Name the failure you are preparing for, identify the recovery point and time you need, and test a small restore sequence.

lessons.title: Project hygiene needs a clean boundary
lessons.deck: Separate what you preserve, what you rebuild, and what you can safely discard.
lessons.summary: A project is easier to maintain when its durable source is clearly separated from local results. Marking that boundary helps you remove generated data without losing the recipe that creates it, and it gives another person a clearer starting point when the work needs to move or be rebuilt.

concepts.analogy: A labeled shelf in a workshop
concepts.definition: An explicit rule that distinguishes files to preserve from files that may be recreated or removed.
concepts.example: Source code and a lockfile stay on the preserve shelf while a local preview folder can be rebuilt.

concepts.analogy: A packing list for finished pieces
concepts.definition: A short record of which generated outputs exist, who uses them, and how they are recreated.
concepts.example: A README can name the preview bundle, its build command, and the folder where the result appears.

concepts.analogy: A fresh workbench with only the materials on the plan
concepts.definition: A project state recreated from its preserved source without relying on accidental local leftovers.
concepts.example: A fresh clone should be able to install its documented dependencies and produce the expected build.

lessons.misconception: A small project is automatically a well-organized project. Size does not show whether its source, generated outputs, and rebuild instructions are distinguishable.
lessons.takeaway: Name the source of truth, list the outputs it creates, and check that a clean checkout can follow the rebuild path.

lessons.title: Privacy needs a stop condition
lessons.deck: A useful record also needs a boundary for when collection ends.
lessons.summary: Privacy is not only about what a record excludes at the start. It also depends on how long the record remains useful and what happens when its purpose ends. A clear stop condition keeps a helpful summary from quietly becoming a permanent history of activity.

concepts.analogy: A library loan period
concepts.definition: The planned period during which information is kept because it still serves its stated purpose.
concepts.example: A recent workflow count may need a few weeks of history, while older detail no longer supports the decision.

concepts.analogy: A name written on the outside of a package
concepts.definition: A piece of information that can reveal more about a person, place, or activity than the task requires.
concepts.example: A file path or message body may identify private work even when a simple count would be enough.

concepts.analogy: A calendar reminder to return the library book
concepts.definition: A specific condition or time that says when data should be removed or reduced.
concepts.example: A report can keep daily totals for trend review and drop older event-level records after the comparison window.

lessons.misconception: Aggregate counts can never be sensitive. A summary can still reveal private activity when its scope, timing, or category is too specific for the purpose.
lessons.takeaway: State the purpose, keep the least revealing useful fields, and define when the record should stop being retained.

lessons.title: Agent work benefits from a narrow task boundary
lessons.deck: A clear scope protects both the result and the work around it.
lessons.summary: An agent can make progress faster when the task names its allowed surface and its protected edges. A narrow boundary does not mean ignoring useful context; it means separating the evidence needed for the decision from unrelated files, actions, or assumptions that could make the change harder to review.

concepts.analogy: The marked area of a construction site
concepts.definition: The files, systems, and actions that a task is allowed to affect.
concepts.example: A dashboard refresh can allow two JSON files while protecting source code and personal folders.

concepts.analogy: A bridge weight limit that must remain true
concepts.definition: A condition that must still hold after the work is complete.
concepts.example: Published lesson offsets remain sequential even when new lessons are appended.

concepts.analogy: A receipt attached to an expense claim
concepts.definition: A small, relevant proof that the intended result and its constraints were checked.
concepts.example: A passing validator and a storage comparison support a routine update without exposing task contents.

lessons.misconception: More context always improves an agent's result. Unrelated context can expand the change surface, blur the acceptance check, and make a safe boundary harder to preserve.
lessons.takeaway: Set the allowed surface, name the invariant, and collect one proof point that directly supports the requested result.

lessons.title: Memory pressure needs a foreground budget
lessons.deck: Protect the work that must stay ready, then reduce competing demand deliberately.
lessons.summary: When the Mac feels crowded, start with the task you are trying to keep responsive. Give that foreground work a simple memory budget, identify the largest competing workload, and make one reversible change. This makes the result easier to judge than closing many small apps at random.

concepts.analogy: A fixed number of seats reserved for the main guest
concepts.definition: A practical limit on how much memory the foreground task should need to remain comfortable.
concepts.example: An editor may need room for the current project and preview, so background exports should not consume the remaining headroom.

concepts.analogy: The tools currently on the workbench
concepts.definition: The portion of a program's data and code currently held in physical memory.
concepts.example: A large project may have a bigger resident set while its editor keeps many assets ready for quick switching.

concepts.analogy: A thermometer watched over the whole afternoon
concepts.definition: The direction and persistence of memory pressure across a comparable period of work.
concepts.example: Pressure that stays high during the same export is a stronger clue than one brief spike during app launch.

lessons.misconception: One brief memory-pressure spike means the Mac is failing. A short burst can be normal; sustained pressure during the same workload is more useful for deciding what to investigate.
lessons.takeaway: Protect the foreground task, identify the largest competing demand, change one thing, and compare the same workload again.

lessons.title: Storage needs a retention reason
lessons.deck: Keep a file because it has a job, not because it happens to be there.
lessons.summary: Storage becomes easier to manage when each large folder has a clear reason to remain. Source material, backups, generated output, and temporary downloads do not all need the same lifetime. Naming the job and review date helps separate useful history from leftovers without turning a storage scan into a guess about what is safe to delete.

concepts.analogy: A label explaining why a box stays on the shelf
concepts.definition: The purpose that justifies keeping a file or folder for a stated period.
concepts.example: A release archive may stay for support while a temporary export can be reviewed after the handoff.

concepts.analogy: A reminder to check a stored suitcase
concepts.definition: A planned time to reconsider whether retained data still serves its purpose.
concepts.example: A project can mark a generated preview for review after the client has approved the source work.

concepts.analogy: The master recipe behind several prepared dishes
concepts.definition: The preserved material treated as authoritative when other copies or outputs are recreated.
concepts.example: Versioned source and its rebuild instructions can remain authoritative while local build output is replaceable.

lessons.misconception: Old or large files are automatically safe to remove. Age and size are clues for review, not proof that the data is disposable or rebuildable.
lessons.takeaway: Give important data a retention reason, mark a review point, and identify the source of truth before considering removal.

lessons.title: Performance starts with the smallest bottleneck
lessons.deck: Find the narrowest slow point before changing the whole workflow.
lessons.summary: A slow result can come from waiting on storage, computation, memory, or another dependency. Start by finding the part that limits progress in the workload you actually care about, then make one focused change and repeat the same check. This keeps a broad performance complaint from turning into a collection of unrelated tweaks.

concepts.analogy: The narrow neck that limits a bottle's flow
concepts.definition: The part of a process that currently limits how quickly the whole process can advance.
concepts.example: If a build spends most of its time waiting for one slow step, improving unrelated steps may not change the total time.

concepts.analogy: The route a delivery actually travels
concepts.definition: The real task, input, and conditions used to judge a system's performance.
concepts.example: The project and build mode used every day are a more useful workload than an unrelated toy example.

concepts.analogy: Turning one faucet at a time
concepts.definition: A deliberate adjustment that targets one suspected cause while leaving other important conditions stable.
concepts.example: Changing one cache setting before rerunning the same build makes its effect easier to interpret.

lessons.misconception: Improving any fast-looking step will make the whole workflow faster. The total result usually changes most when the current limiting step changes.
lessons.takeaway: Use the real workload, locate its current bottleneck, change one relevant condition, and compare the same task again.
